title: Core of the Truehearted 11
content:
Jiang Cheng stood frozen in shock for what felt like an eternity before finally snapping: “What kind of complete and utter nonsense are you spewing?!”

Wen Ning sounded deceptively calm. “I’m not talking nonsense.”

“Shut your mouth!” Jiang Cheng barked. “My golden core… my golden core was—”

“Restored by Baoshan Sanren.”

“How the hell do you know that?” Jiang Cheng hissed. “Did he even tell you about this?”

“No,” Wen Ning said softly. “Young Master Wei never breathed a word about it to anyone. I know because I saw it with my own eyes.”

A bitter, unhinged sneer pulled across Jiang Cheng’s bloodshot face. “Bullshit! You were there? How could you have possibly been there?! I walked up that mountain completely alone! There is no way you followed me!”

“I didn't follow you,” Wen Ning replied. “I was already up on that mountain from the very beginning.”

The blue veins along Jiang Cheng’s temples bulged violently. “...Liar!”

“Listen to me, then, and tell me if I’m lying!” Wen Ning’s voice hardened. “When you went up that mountain, your eyes were wrapped in black silk. You were feeling your way with a long wooden stick. Just before you reached the summit, you stumbled through a labyrinth of stone spires. It took you nearly an entire hour just to navigate your way out.”

A sudden, minute tremor twitched across Jiang Cheng’s face.

Wen Ning pressed on, relentless. “Then you heard the ringing of a bell. The chimes startled an entire flock of birds into the sky. You tightened your grip on that stick, holding it like you’d hold a sword. The moment the bell went silent, a cold blade was pressed against your chest, and a woman’s voice warned you not to take another step.”

Jiang Cheng had begun to shake like a leaf.

Wen Ning projected his voice, cutting through the cold night air: “You froze instantly. You were terrified, but underneath it all, you were trembling with desperate anticipation. The woman kept her voice pitched low, demanding to know who you were and how you’d managed to find the hidden path. And you answered—”

“Shut up!” Jiang Cheng roared.

Wen Ning roared right back, voice cracking with raw intensity: “...You answered that you were the son of Cangse Sanren, Wei Ying! You told her your home had been put to the torch, that Lotus Pier was drowned in blood, and that Wen Zhuliu, the Core-Melting Hand, had completely dissolved your golden core! That woman grilled you relentlessly about your parents, and right as you answered the very last question, a sweet fragrance drifted into the air—and you dropped unconscious!”

Jiang Cheng looked like he was about to clamp his hands over his ears, his voice fraying into raw desperation: “How do you know that? How the hell could you possibly know that?!”

“Haven't I already told you? Because I was there,” Wen Ning said. “And I wasn't the only one. Young Master Wei was there, too. And along with the two of us, my sister, Wen Qing, was right beside him. The truth is, on that entire godforsaken mountain, there were only three people waiting for you.

“Sect Leader Jiang, did you honestly believe that barren rock was some mystical hidden sanctuary belonging to Baoshan Sanren? Even Young Master Wei hadn't the faintest clue where in the world she actually resided! His mother, Cangse Sanren, never whispered a single detail about her secluded master to a boy that young! That mountain was nothing more than a deserted wasteland outside Yiling!”

Jiang Cheng screamed at the top of his lungs, clinging frantically to the same broken words as if pure, unfiltered hostility could plug the terrifying void in his vocabulary: “Nonsense! That’s enough of your fucking lies! If that’s true, then why was my core restored?!”

“Your golden core was never restored!” Wen Ning shouted. “It was dissolved! Burned away by Wen Zhuliu down to the last trace! The only reason you thought it was healed was because my sister—Wen Qing, the most brilliant physician of the Qishan Wen Sect—cut out Young Master Wei’s golden core and put it into your body!”

Jiang Cheng’s face went totally blank for a heartbeat. “...Put it into me?”

“Yes!” Wen Ning’s voice cracked with righteous fury. “Why do you think he never unsheathed Suibian again?! Why do you think he stopped wearing his sword on his hip altogether?! Did you truly buy that arrogant, rebellious act of his? Did you honestly think he enjoyed having people point at his back, sneering that he was an ill-mannered, undisciplined rogue?!

“It was because wearing it was useless! Because if he carried his sword to all those banquets and night-hunts, people would inevitably challenge him to duels and exhibition matches. And without his golden core, without a sliver of spiritual power to feed the blade, the second he pulled it from its scabbard, his spiritual reserves would dry up in an instant…!”

Jiang Cheng stood there as stiff as a corpse. His eyes took on a sickly, feverish glare, and his lips trembled violently. Forgetting all about Zidian, he abruptly tossed Suibian aside and hurled a frantic, heavy palm strike straight into Wen Ning’s sternum, shrieking like a wounded animal: “Liar!”

Wen Ning took the concussive blow without flinching, stumbling back barely two paces. He calmly scooped Suibian off the dirt, slid the blade back into its scabbard, and shoved the hilt right back into Jiang Cheng’s chest. “Take it!”

Jiang Cheng’s fingers curled around the scabbard on pure, mindless instinct. He didn't move; instead, his gaze drifted uncontrollably toward Wei Wuxian.

And looking upon him was his absolute undoing. Seeing Wei Wuxian slumped over, deathly pale, with dark crimson still drying around his slack lips, hit Jiang Cheng like a sledgehammer to the ribs. Worse still, the look Lan Wangji was aiming at him was so profoundly, lethally arctic that it felt like dropping straight into an abyss of black ice.

Wen Ning said, “Take that sword. March into the banquet hall, take it to the training grounds, take it to every single corner of this place! Order every man, woman, and disciple you cross paths with to try and draw that blade! See if a single soul on this earth can pull an inch of steel from that sheath! Then you’ll know whether I’m lying to you or not!

“Sect Leader Jiang—you’ve always been so painfully, desperately competitive. You’ve spent your entire life measuring yourself against everyone else. But do you understand now? You were never going to beat him. Not in this lifetime!”

Jiang Cheng lashed out with a vicious kick, sending Wen Ning reeling, before gripping Suibian with white knuckles and bolting toward the banquet hall like a madman.

He stumbled down the winding corridors, shrieking and howling into the night. The kick had sent Wen Ning crashing against an ornamental tree in the courtyard. He pushed himself upright slowly, shaking off the impact, and immediately turned back to check on the other two.

Lan Wangji’s ethereal face was carved from pure, bloodless stone, his expression terrifyingly grim. He cast one final, lingering look at the ancestral hall of the Yunmeng Jiang Sect, hitched the unconscious Wei Wuxian securely against his back, and turned on his heel without looking back.

“Young... Young Master Lan,” Wen Ning stammered, scrambling to keep up. “Where are you going?”

Lan Wangji’s boots paused right at the edge of the stone steps.

“Earlier,” he said, his voice dropping low, “he asked me to take him away.”

Wen Ning hurried after him, trailing in their wake as they slipped past the grand gates of Lotus Pier.

Down at the water, the chaotic fleet that had carried the battered sects downstream had long since disbanded, their vessels returning home. All that remained tied to the wooden piers were a few weathered, unmanned commuter skiffs. Long, slender, and shaped like willow leaves, the boats had gently upturned bows and could carry roughly seven or eight passengers, with a pair of long oars resting across the stern.

Carrying Wei Wuxian on his back, Lan Wangji stepped aboard without a moment’s hesitation. Wen Ning vaulted onto the stern, naturally taking hold of the oars. With two clean, measured strokes, the little wooden boat glided smoothly into open water, catching the river's current as it drifted away from the illuminated docks and melted into the dark belly of the river.

Lan Wangji leaned Wei Wuxian gently against his chest, carefully feeding him two medicinal pills and watching his throat until he was certain they had gone down. Only then did he produce a clean handkerchief, softly dabbing away the dried blood crusting around his pale mouth and jaw.

Suddenly, a small, nervous voice broke the quiet: “Young... Young Master Lan.”

Lan Wangji didn't look up. “What is it?”

All the unyielding defiance Wen Ning had unleashed against Jiang Cheng had evaporated into thin air. Swallowing his nerves, he mumbled timidly, “Please... please don't tell Young Master Wei that I spilled the truth about the golden core. He gave me strict, furious orders never to breathe a single word of it to a soul. I know we can’t keep it hidden forever, but I...”

After a beat of heavy silence, Lan Wangji murmured, “Do not worry.”

Wen Ning seemed to let out a long breath of relief—even if dead lungs had no real breath to give. “Thank you, Young Master Lan,” he said earnestly.

Lan Wangji gave a slight, dismissive shake of his head.

Wen Ning continued softly, “Thank you for speaking up for my sister and me back on Koi Tower all those years ago. I’ve never forgotten it. When I lost control afterward... I truly am so, so sorry.”

Lan Wangji offered no reply.

Wen Ning added, “And thank you even more for looking after A-Yuan all these years.”

At that name, Lan Wangji’s pale gaze flicked upward.

“I honestly thought my entire bloodline was wiped out,” Wen Ning murmured. “Not a single one left. I never dared to dream that A-Yuan could still be alive. He looks so much like my cousin did in his twenties.”

“He was hidden inside a hollow tree trunk for too long,” Lan Wangji said quietly. “He ran a dangerous fever. A prolonged illness.”

Wen Ning nodded in quiet understanding. “I figured it had to be a severe fever. He doesn't remember a thing from his childhood. I chatted with him for quite a while back on the boat, and he wouldn't stop talking about you.” A touch of dejection crept into his voice. “Back in the day, he’d only ever babble about Young Master Wei... Not that he ever talked about me anyway.”

“You did not tell him,” Lan Wangji noted.

“About his real identity? No. I didn't.”

Wen Ning turned his back toward them, putting his back into the oars as they cut through the current. “He has a good life right now. Handing him the truth, saddling him with memories far too heavy to carry... it would only ruin the peace he has now.”

Lan Wangji said softly, “He will have to know eventually.”

Wen Ning went quiet for a moment, then sighed. “Yes. He’ll find out sooner or later.” He lifted his eyes toward the murky night sky. “Just like Young Master Wei and Sect Leader Jiang. Sect Leader Jiang was bound to learn the truth about the core transfer eventually. Young Master Wei couldn't have kept that from him for an entire lifetime.”

The night hung dead and still, the dark water murmuring beneath the hull.

Suddenly, Lan Wangji’s voice cut through the dark: “Did it hurt?”

Wen Ning blinked. “What?”

“Carving out the core,” Lan Wangji said, his voice dropping to a gravelly murmur. “Was it painful?”

“If I told you it wasn't,” Wen Ning replied softly, “you wouldn't believe me anyway, would you?”

Lan Wangji’s brow twitched. “I assumed Wen Qing would have had a method.”

“Before we climbed that mountain, my sister brewed every anesthetic and numbing agent she knew, desperate to dull the agony,” Wen Ning explained. “But when the time came, she realized none of it could be used. If the body is sedated while a golden core is being severed from the spiritual veins, the core itself is corrupted. There’s no guarantee it won't destabilize and dissolve into nothing on the spot.”

Lan Wangji’s breath hitched. “...So?”

Wen Ning’s rhythm on the oars hitched for a fraction of a second. “So... the person having their core carved out had to remain completely conscious.”

Completely conscious.

Forced to stay wide awake, watching as the core tethered to his very soul was brutally sliced and unraveled from his meridians. Feeling that boundless, surging sea of spiritual power slowly ebb away—quieting, dimming, decaying—until it became a stagnant, dead pool that would never stir a ripple again.

A suffocating silence descended over the boat. When Lan Wangji finally managed to speak, his voice was a ragged, raw rasp, the first few words trembling uncontrollably:

“...Awake the entire time?”

“Two nights and one day,” Wen Ning whispered. “Wide awake.”

Lan Wangji asked, “What were the odds of success back then?”

“Around fifty percent.”

“Fifty percent.” Lan Wangji drew in a silent, shuddering breath, his head dropping as he repeated the number like a curse: “...Fifty percent.”

His arm tightened around Wei Wuxian’s shoulders so fiercely that his knuckles turned an ivory white.

Wen Ning continued, “After all, nobody had ever successfully attempted a core transfer before. My sister had written a theoretical treatise on the procedure years ago, but it was purely hypothetical; she’d never had a living subject to test it on. The older clan elders dismissed her research as a mad delusion. Besides, it was completely impractical—who in their right mind would ever volunteer to cut out their own golden core and hand it to someone else? Doing that means signing away your future, reducing yourself to a crippled half-mortal who can never climb the peaks of cultivation again.

“So when Young Master Wei tracked us down and begged her to do it, my sister flatly refused. She warned him that theory was one thing, but carving open a living chest was another, and that she had less than half a chance of pulling it off.

“But Young Master Wei wouldn't let it go. He hounded her relentlessly, insisting that fifty-fifty was plenty good enough. He said even if it failed and his core was ruined, he was resourceful enough to carve out another path. But Sect Leader Jiang couldn't. Sect Leader Jiang was far too proud, far too obsessed with winning and losing. His cultivation was his entire life. If he had to spend the rest of his days as a mediocre nobody, he’d be broken forever.”

Lan Wangji lowered his eyes, his pale, glass-like gaze fixing entirely on the sleeping face resting against his chest. Slowly, he reached out a hand, his fingertips hovering for a long, tender second before brushing infinitesimally against Wei Wuxian’s cheek.

Wen Ning glanced over his shoulder, unable to help himself. “Young Master Lan... you don't seem entirely shocked by this. Did you... did you already know?”

A bitter, aching rasp tore through Lan Wangji’s throat: “I only knew... that his spiritual energy had suffered some grave anomaly.”

He had never imagined the truth could be this monstrous.

Wen Ning murmured, “If it wasn't because of this...”

If it wasn't because he had run out of roads to walk.

Right then, the head lolling against Lan Wangji’s shoulder gave a faint, restless twitch. Wei Wuxian’s dark lashes fluttered against his skin, slowly peeling open as consciousness returned.
